x: LPG is mainly propane (C₃H₈) and butane (C₄H₁₀), liquefied under pressure. Methane is CNG, and CO + H₂ + N₂ is producer gas.
t: Discriminate LPG (propane/butane) from CNG (methane).

x: Option C is incorrect: biogas comes from anaerobic digestion, meaning without oxygen, of organic waste. The coal, hydrogen and LPG descriptions are right.
t: Recall that biogas forms without oxygen.

x: Both are true and R explains A: hydrogen gives only water when used, with no carbon, CO, SO₂ or particles, which makes it the cleanest fuel.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Both are true: the octane number rates petrol's resistance to knocking in spark engines, and the cetane number rates diesel's ignition quality.
t: Discriminate octane (petrol) from cetane (diesel).

x: I and III are correct: natural gas is 70–90% methane, and producer gas is CO, H₂ and N₂. II is false because biogas is 50–75% methane and 25–50% CO₂; the ranges are swapped.
t: Check gas percentages for a swap.

x: Petrol runs spark-ignition engines, diesel compression-ignition engines, kerosene lamps, stoves and jets, and hydrogen fuel cells and rockets, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
t: Recall the use of each fuel.

x: Hydrogen gives about 1,50,000 kJ/kg, LPG 55,000, coal 25,000–33,000 and cow-dung cake 6,000–8,000, giving a-i, b-iii, c-iv, d-ii.
t: Recall the calorific value ladder.

x: Knocking is early auto-ignition of the petrol–air mix, causing a metallic knock, lost power and engine damage.
t: Recall the meaning of knocking.

x: Both are true and R explains A: CNG and LPG burn more completely, giving far less CO, unburnt hydrocarbons and soot, though they still release CO₂.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: All four raise octane number: tetraethyl lead (now banned), MTBE, ethanol and toluene.
t: Recall the anti-knock agents.

x: All four are correct: petrol is C₅–C₁₀ (alkanes, alkenes and aromatics), diesel C₁₅–C₁₈ and kerosene C₁₀–C₁₆.
t: Recall the carbon ranges of petroleum fractions.

x: Both are true: biogas contains traces of H₂S and H₂, and coal contains hydrogen, oxygen, sulphur and nitrogen besides carbon.
t: Recall the composition of fuels.

x: Hydrogen is pure H₂, water gas CO + H₂, producer gas CO + H₂ + N₂, and coal contains C, H, O, S and N, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Discriminate water gas from producer gas.

x: Petrol, diesel and kerosene are liquid fossil fuels from crude oil, CNG is a gas from gas fields, wood and dung are solid biomass, and ethanol and biodiesel are liquid biofuels, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
t: Classify fuels by state and source.

x: CNG gives about 50,000 kJ/kg, petrol 45,000–48,000, kerosene and diesel about 45,000 and biogas 35,000–40,000, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall the calorific value ladder.

x: Both are true and R explains A: at 17,000–22,000 kJ/kg wood gives much less energy than coal or gas, so its calorific value counts as low.
t: Check whether R supports A.

x: CNG runs buses and cars, LPG domestic cooking and heating, biogas rural cooking and lighting, and coal thermal power plants, giving a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii.
t: Recall the use of each fuel.

x: All three are correct: petrol and diesel emit CO₂, CO, NOₓ, hydrocarbons and particles, diesel emits more soot, and coal pollutes most.
t: Recall the pollutants from each fuel.

x: Ethanol is blended as E10 or E20 (10% or 20%), which raises octane and cuts emissions. India targets E20.
t: Recall India's ethanol blending targets.

x: I and II are correct: iso-octane is the reference at 100 and n-heptane at 0. III is false because n-heptane, which knocks badly, is 0, not 100.
t: Recall the octane reference fuels.

x: Cetane (n-hexadecane) ignites easily and is the reference at 100 on the cetane scale.
t: Recall the cetane reference fuel.

x: Both are true and R explains A: TEL was phased out because the lead it released is toxic.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Both are true and R explains A: burning biogas gives mainly CO₂ with only traces of H₂S, so its emissions are low.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Two are keyed: wood and cow-dung burnt in homes give smoke, CO and particles that cause indoor air pollution. Biogas burns clean, and coal is mainly treated as an outdoor polluter.
t: Discriminate traditional biomass fuels from clean fuels.

x: Petrol (45,000–48,000 kJ/kg) and kerosene or diesel (about 45,000 kJ/kg) are nearly equal in calorific value. The other pairs differ widely.
t: Recall the calorific value ladder.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: SO₂, NOₓ and ash are extra pollutants; coal's high CO₂ comes from its high carbon content.
t: Check whether R is a cause or a list of other effects.
